title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Galatians
author: Severianus of Gabala
addressee: Christian readers, especially those tempted to keep the Mosaic law
occasion: Catena fragments explaining Paul's Letter to the Galatians, written to counter the view that Gentile believers should judaize and keep the law.
argument: Severianus explains that Paul wrote Galatians because some from the circumcision were persuading Gentile believers to judaize, even though the apostles had already ruled against imposing the law. He argues that the law was a temporary, bodily discipline that could not save or give life, while grace and faith in Christ bring freedom and a heavenly citizenship. The law was given to teach the mind to recognize sin and prepare people for grace, but after Christ it is obsolete. Baptism, not law-keeping, makes Jews and Gentiles equal by clothing them all in Christ. Paul's varied tone of rebuke, exhortation, accusation, and lament comes from the passion of his grief and his affection for the Galatians, and his use of 'allegory' really means prophecy enacted through events, as with Hagar and Sarah.

outline.move: Introduces the occasion of Galatians, the Antioch ruling, and Paul's defense of his gospel against judaizing teachers.
Explains Paul's confrontation with Peter, the law's bodily works, death to the law, life in Christ, and the law's role in exposing sin and preparing for grace.
Discusses baptism's equalizing power, the danger of returning to sabbaths and festivals, Paul's loving tone, and the meaning of allegory as prophecy through events.
Explains Sinai, Hagar, and the earthly Jerusalem as slavery, contrasts heavenly freedom, and treats the flesh-spirit conflict, sowing to the flesh, and the new creation.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of Galatians, defending his gospel of grace against law-keeping.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle addressed by Paul in Galatians 2, accused of annulling the apostolic decree with his own teaching.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: The lawgiver, cited as an example of prophecy through actions.

cast.name: Jeremiah
cast.who: The prophet whose linen girdle is cited as prophecy through both actions and words.

cast.name: the Hagarites
cast.who: Descendants of Hagar and Ishmael, linked to Sinai and slavery.

cast.name: Ishmael
cast.who: Mentioned only as the ancestor of the Hagarites, whose descendants inhabit the desert near Sinai.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by φησίν or φησί, or by direct quotation of Galatians

key_terms.sense: The Mosaic law, especially its bodily commands about food, sabbath, and circumcision
God's gift of salvation in Christ, contrasted with law-keeping
To adopt Jewish practices, especially law-keeping, by Gentile believers
Circumcision, the mark of the old covenant and the judaizing demand
Uncircumcision, representing Gentile believers not under the law
Faith in Christ, the means of justification and new life
In this work, prophecy enacted through historical events, not a departure from literal history
The weak and poor elements of the old order, including law-observances and pagan worship
The new creation in Christ, replacing circumcision and uncircumcision
The flesh, the sphere of bodily law-keeping and sinful desire
To be justified or made righteous, not by works of law but by faith
God's promises, especially to Abraham, fulfilled in Christ

scripture: Severianus cites the Septuagint and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. He refers to 'the Song of Songs' (Ἄσματα τῶν Ἀσμάτων), 'the letter to the Romans' (πρὸς Ῥωμαίους), and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and LXX Psalm numbering where applicable.
uncertain: The exact date of composition beyond the broad late 4th–early 5th century range.
Whether the fragments preserve Severianus's original wording or have been adapted by the catena compiler.
The precise identity of the 'some from the circumcision' beyond their role as judaizing teachers.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul's varied tone of rebuke, exhortation, accusation, and lament comes from the passion of his grief and his affection for the Galatians
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τῆς γὰρ ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος συνεχῶς αὐτὸν μεταβάλλειν ἀναγκάζει τοῦ λόγου τὸ εἶδος, καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐπιτιμᾶν, νῦν δὲ παρακαλεῖν, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν κατηγορεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ θρηνεῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says the passion of grief (τῆς ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος) forces Paul to change the form of his discourse continually—now rebuking, now exhorting, now accusing, now lamenting. The brief should not attribute this solely to 'affection for the Galatians' but to the passion of his grief/anguish.

_unresolved_facts.claim: his use of 'allegory' really means prophecy enacted through events, as with Hagar and Sarah
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ οὖν δι' ἔργων προφητεία ἀλληγορία νῦν ὠνόμασται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Severianus says that prophecy through works/deeds (δι' ἔργων προφητεία) is now called allegory, not that allegory 'really means' prophecy through events. He distinguishes this from true allegory which does not follow the literal text (οὐ στοιχεῖ τοῖς ῥητοῖς). The brief conflates his technical distinction.

_unresolved_facts.name: Peter
_unresolved_facts.claim: accused of annulling the apostolic decree with his own teaching
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: σὺ κατέλυσας αὐτὰ δόγματι ὅπερ ἀπεστάλη παρ' ὑμῶν τοῖς Ἀντιοχεῦσι καὶ πάσῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ. ἀπρεπὲς οὖν ταύτα διδάσκειν ἑτέρους, ὧν τῆς ἐπιμελείας ἀπέστης καὶ ἰδίῳ κατέλυσας δόγματι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says Peter dissolved/annulled (κατέλυσας) with his own dogma what was sent from them to the Antiochenes and all the world, and it is unseemly for him to teach others what he abandoned. The brief's 'accused of annulling the apostolic decree with his own teaching' is not quite right—it's that he annulled the decree by his own dogma/teaching, not that he was 'accused of' this by Paul in the fragment's representation.

_unresolved_facts.name: Moses
_unresolved_facts.claim: cited as an example of prophecy through actions
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: αἱ δὲ δι' ἔργων μόνον ὡς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Moses is cited as an example of prophecy through works/deeds alone (δι' ἔργων μόνον), not 'prophecy through actions' as a general category. The brief's phrasing obscures that this is one of three types of prophecy Severianus enumerates (words only, deeds only, both words and deeds).
The name 'Sina' does not appear in the source text. The source has Σινᾶ (Sinai) throughout. This names entry appears to be fabricated or imported from elsewhere.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He refers to 'the Song of Songs' (Ἄσματα τῶν Ἀσμάτων)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source has τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων ('that in the Songs of Songs'), not a standalone reference to 'the Song of Songs' as a book title. The brief's claim about what 'he refers to' is inaccurate.
Isaiah is not quoted or mentioned in the source text. The brief incorrectly states that Severianus quotes Isaiah.
